strengths: The paper makes a practically important Algorithms/General contribution: it adapts pretrained diffusion transformers to substantially more compressed latent spaces through post-training, avoiding the cost of training large text-to-image models from scratch.

The embedding-alignment stage is simple and empirically consequential. Table 6 shows that removing it causes catastrophic failure for DiT-XL and SANA and degrades FLUX, while Fig. 4 provides supporting representation-level analysis.

The evaluation spans three model families and both class-conditional and text-conditional generation. DC-Gen-DiT improves ImageNet gFID while increasing throughput by roughly 4×, and the SANA/FLUX adaptations largely preserve the reported CLIP and GenEval scores.

The efficiency gains are substantial and resolution-dependent in the expected direction. On one H100, DC-Gen-FLUX reduces reported 4K latency from 213.81 s to 4.04 s; the method is also complementary to quantization.

The paper includes useful ablations of embedding alignment, LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and the modified objective for guidance-distilled FLUX. The derivation motivating the latter is clear, and the manuscript is generally well organized.
weaknesses: The evidence for the central claim of preserving FLUX/SANA perceptual quality is incomplete. At 1024×1024, the main evaluation relies primarily on CLIP score and GenEval, which do not adequately measure realism, aesthetics, artifacts, or distributional fidelity. There is no human preference study, strong perceptual-quality benchmark, or full-dataset FID comparison against the base models; several ablations use only 1,000 MJHQ samples.

The strongest 4K claim is insufficiently validated. Only four selected DC-Gen-FLUX samples are presented, with no quantitative or human evaluation at 2K/4K. Moreover, the manuscript says the base FLUX model does not natively support 4K while simultaneously benchmarking it at 4K; the precise generation protocol and fairness of this comparison need clarification.

Several implementation details needed for reproduction are missing: the size and construction of the synthetic training set, prompt sources and filtering, base-model sampling settings, resolution curriculum, latent normalization, spatial downsampling operator used for alignment, exact loss for output-head alignment, LoRA insertion locations, and inference step/scheduler/guidance settings. The modified guidance-distillation objective also does not state whether gradients pass through the unconditional branch or how its assumed raw-velocity behavior is maintained during fine-tuning.

The reported 53× and 138× headline speedups conflate multiple changes. The 2K/4K variant uses DC-AE-f64 rather than the f32 model used at lower resolution, while the 5090 result additionally uses quantization and avoids CPU offloading. These are useful system results, but clearer component-wise latency, memory, autoencoder encode/decode cost, batch-size, and quality-matched comparisons are needed.

The claimed 520× training-cost reduction in Fig. 2 compares against heterogeneous historical models with different architectures, datasets, objectives, hardware eras, and target quality. This is not a controlled comparison and should not be presented as direct evidence of algorithmic efficiency.

The qualitative comparisons appear prompt-selected and use few examples. No variance across seeds, failure cases, challenging compositional prompts, typography benchmark, or analysis of information loss from deep compression is provided. Possible biases inherited through synthetic data and limitations of the approach are also not discussed.

strengths: The central practical idea is useful: adapting pretrained diffusion transformers to deeply compressed latent spaces can reduce token counts without the prohibitive cost of retraining large models from scratch.

The embedding-alignment stage is simple and empirically important. Figure 3 and Table 6 show severe instability under direct fine-tuning and large improvements when alignment is introduced across DiT, SANA, and FLUX, supporting applicability beyond one architecture.

The efficiency gains are substantial. The reported H100 results show roughly 4× higher throughput at 1K and much larger gains at 2K/4K; the ImageNet experiments also demonstrate improved throughput and competitive gFID.

The paper includes useful ablations of embedding alignment, LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and the corrected objective for guidance-distilled FLUX. The derivation of that corrected velocity target is clear and practically relevant.

The method is presented clearly, and the appendix supplies core optimization hyperparameters and numerous qualitative comparisons. Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best viewed as Applied/Systems rather than a fundamentally new generative algorithm; under that framing, its practical scope and potential impact are notable.
weaknesses: The main claim that generation quality remains comparable to the base models is not adequately established. At 1024 resolution, Table 2 reports only CLIP score and GenEval, which primarily measure alignment/compositionality and do not substantiate perceptual quality, realism, diversity, or distributional fidelity. There is no human preference study, strong perceptual metric, or sufficiently broad blinded evaluation.

The headline 2K/4K claims receive especially weak quality validation. Only a small number of selected qualitative examples are shown, with no human evaluation or quantitative high-resolution assessment. Moreover, FLUX.1-Krea is described as not natively supporting 4K, making its direct 4K extrapolation an unconvincing quality baseline even though it remains informative for raw computational scaling.

The speed evaluation omits important details needed for a fair systems comparison, including sampling steps and solver, numerical precision, exact batch sizes, compilation settings, warm-up protocol, and whether all encoder/decoder and text-processing costs are consistently included. The 138× claim on RTX 5090 additionally compares against a baseline requiring CPU offloading, so much of that gain comes from the combined quantization/memory configuration rather than DC-Gen alone.

The core alignment evidence compares primarily against randomly initialized patch/output layers followed by direct fine-tuning. Stronger transfer baselines are missing, such as alternative structured initialization, feature distillation, progressive compression, freezing schedules, or carefully stabilized direct fine-tuning. There is also no ablation separating patch-embedder alignment from output-head alignment or measuring their individual costs.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the hyperparameter table. The paper does not adequately specify the synthetic training dataset—prompt source, number of examples, filtering, generation settings, resolution distribution, or release status—nor LoRA insertion locations, inference settings, evaluation seeds, or uncertainty across runs. These omissions are consequential because both quality preservation and training stability may depend strongly on these choices.

The comparison claiming a 520× training-cost reduction against DALL·E 2 is not well controlled: it contrasts post-training of an already capable 12B model with from-scratch training of different models, datasets, objectives, and hardware assumptions. It does not isolate the cost required to obtain the underlying FLUX model and therefore overstates what can be inferred.

The work largely combines an existing deeply compressed autoencoder with a straightforward feature-alignment and LoRA adaptation pipeline. This is potentially valuable as systems work, but the conceptual novelty is moderate, and the current evaluation is not rigorous enough to compensate fully. Overall, the efficiency case is persuasive, but the central quality-preservation and high-resolution claims remain insufficiently supported, leading to a slight preference for rejection.

The lightweight embedding-alignment stage is simple and well motivated. The ImageNet ablation is particularly persuasive: direct adaptation becomes unstable, whereas alignment produces stable training and strong gFID, supporting the claimed mechanism rather than merely reporting an engineering recipe.

The evaluation spans meaningfully different settings—class-conditional DiT and text-to-image SANA and FLUX—providing evidence that the approach is not tied to one architecture. The gains are consistent: approximately 4× throughput at 1K, with much larger reductions in measured high-resolution latency.

The efficiency–quality trade-off is compelling. At 1024×1024, DC-Gen-SANA and DC-Gen-FLUX retain similar CLIP scores and match or improve GenEval relative to their base models, while the qualitative comparisons generally preserve realism, composition, multilingual generation, and text rendering.

The paper includes useful component studies covering embedding alignment, LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and the corrected objective for guidance-distilled FLUX. Training hyperparameters and hardware-specific latency/throughput results are also reported.

The guidance-distillation correction is technically sensible and broadens the framework's usefulness for adapting publicly available distilled models. Overall, this is a relevant and potentially high-impact systems/algorithmic contribution to efficient high-resolution generation.
weaknesses: The strongest 53×–138× headline results are not supported by equally strong quality evaluation at 2K and 4K. These settings use a more compressed f64 autoencoder and additional high-resolution training, while the base FLUX model is acknowledged not to support native 4K generation. Thus, the 4K comparison is not a clean quality-matched acceleration experiment; high-resolution perceptual metrics, human preference studies, and comparisons against tiled or other practical 4K baselines are needed.

Text-to-image quality evidence at 1K is narrow. CLIP score and GenEval do not adequately measure realism, fine detail, diversity, or degradation caused by aggressive latent compression. No human evaluation is reported, and the qualitative figures contain relatively few curated prompts.

Some ablations use only 1,000 MJHQ samples, making the modest quantitative differences between LoRA/full tuning and the two objectives potentially noisy. Repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and evaluation on the full set would strengthen these conclusions.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript does not adequately specify the size, prompt construction, filtering, or release status of the synthetic training data; exact inference samplers and step counts; LoRA insertion details; or all resolution-specific training configurations. The stated intention to export models is helpful but not equivalent to an explicit code, model, and data-release commitment.

The method is related to straightforward feature distillation/alignment followed by parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Its originality is therefore moderate, and comparisons with alternative latent-transfer strategies—such as learned adapters, joint encoder/decoder alignment, or direct distillation from the base model—are limited.

The computational accounting emphasizes GPU-days but does not fully report alignment-versus-fine-tuning costs, memory usage, or the cost of producing the synthetic dataset. The 5090 result is also strongly influenced by SVDQuant eliminating CPU offloading, so the 138× figure should be presented primarily as a combined systems result rather than an isolated benefit of DC-Gen.
